text:
Deloitte Data Engineer Round 2: The Interview I’ll Never Forget 🚀🔥
Last Thursday, 9:02 AM.
 Round 2.
 The real technical round.
 The round where you either prove your experience… or you’re out.
The interviewer started with a smile and said:
 “Let’s go deeper. Round 1 was just the warm-up.”
At that moment, I knew this wasn’t going to be about definitions.
 It was going to be about judgment, architecture, debugging, and real-world chaos.
Here are the exact Round 2 questions Deloitte asked me — and how I approached them calmly when most people panic.
1️⃣ “Design an end-to-end data platform for a fintech system.”
I explained a Lakehouse setup with Kafka + ADF + Delta + Databricks + Unity Catalog.
 Real-time + batch in one clean flow.
2️⃣ “Write a SQL to remove duplicates and keep the latest row.”
Used ROW_NUMBER with timestamp ordering.
 Simple. Clear. Trusted.
3️⃣ “Pipeline is successful but data is wrong. What do you check first?”
I said: row count, logs, joins, schema drift, checkpoint issues.
 They nodded immediately.
4️⃣ “How will you build a data quality framework?”
I shared my metadata-driven rule engine with a quarantine zone.
 This answer lands strong.
5️⃣ “Spark job takes 40 mins. Bring it under 10.”
Broadcast joins, AQE, repartition strategy, caching, cluster tuning.
 This answer alone filled half the interview.
6️⃣ “Incremental load without last_modified_date?”
Hash-based change tracking.
 They loved this.
7️⃣ “How do you handle duplicate Kafka events in streaming?”
Dedup with eventId + watermark + idempotent MERGE.
8️⃣ “Explain a 2 AM real production issue you solved.”
Logs → isolate partition → quarantine → fix → reprocess → RCA.
 Nothing impresses more than real experience.
By the end of the round, the interviewer said:
 “You think like an engineer, not just a coder. That’s what we look for.”
That sentence stayed with me.
Here’s the truth:
 Companies like Deloitte don’t care how many definitions you memorized.
 They care about your:
 • clarity
 • debugging sense
 • ownership
 • and ability to work under pressure
That’s what actually gets you selected.

text:
🔥 Completed One More Data Engineering Interview This Week!

This Week I had another Data Engineering interview, and I’m sharing a couple of important questions I was asked. Posting here so it helps others preparing for Azure + PySpark + SQL roles.

✅ 1️⃣ SQL Question: Identify Employees Sitting on Multiple Floors

📌 Requirement:
If an employee sits on multiple floors → print ‘Multiple’, else print the exact floor number.

SELECT emp,
 CASE 
 WHEN COUNT(DISTINCT floor) > 1 THEN 'Multiple'
 ELSE MAX(floor)
 END AS floor
FROM emp_table
GROUP BY emp
ORDER BY emp;

✅ 2️⃣ PySpark Question: Find Student Who Scored Highest Marks in Class 10

📌 Check at class level, not subject level.

from pyspark.sql import functions as F
from pyspark.sql.window import Window

# Step 1: Total marks per student per class
student_total = (df.groupBy("class_id", "student_id")
 .agg(F.sum("marks").alias("total_marks")))

# Step 2: Rank students within class
w = Window.partitionBy("class_id").orderBy(F.desc("total_marks"))

result = (student_total
 .withColumn("rank", F.dense_rank().over(w))
 .filter((F.col("class_id") == 10) & (F.col("rank") == 1)))

result.show()

💡 Good interview overall — covered SQL aggregation logic and PySpark window functions.

If you’re preparing for Azure Data Engineer or PySpark-heavy roles, these scenarios are very common.

Happy Learning! 🚀

text:
Quick SQL question for everyone…

We all use column aliases to make queries cleaner. But have you noticed this?

You can use an alias in ORDER BY, but you can’t use it in WHERE.

Example:

SELECT salary * 12 AS annual_salary
FROM employees
ORDER BY annual_salary; -- works

But this fails:

SELECT salary * 12 AS annual_salary
FROM employees
WHERE annual_salary > 500000; -- alias not allowed here

Why do you think SQL allows aliases in ORDER BY but not in WHERE?

Curious to hear everyone’s thoughts.

author: Sujeet Mohanty
headline: Senior Data Engineer @ Accenture
text:
When SQL starts looking like ancient scripture…

Since last week, I’ve been trying to understand the flow of a stored procedure that’s nearly 5,000 lines long.
Unorganised.
Unformatted.
No comments.
Just pure SQL chaos.

At this point, I’m convinced that understanding this code should count as a separate skill on my resume.
Smoke is literally coming out of my ears — my notebook looks like a crime scene, and my laptop is judging me silently. 😅

But on a serious note…

👉 Clean code is not a luxury — it’s a responsibility.
👉 We write code once, but someone else reads and maintains it for years.
👉 A few minutes of formatting, meaningful naming, and comments can save hours (or days!) of confusion later.

If your future teammate is pulling their hair out because of your code…
Did you even code? 😄

Here’s to writing cleaner, readable, and more maintainable SQL — for our sanity and for everyone who comes after us. ✨
